Southern short-tailed shrew (Blarina carolinensis) is among the smallest terrestrial mammals in eastern North America, and its life history reflects the intense energetic demands of a high-metabolism insectivore. Respirometry trials conducted under standard thermal conditions demonstrate that the basal metabolic rate of this species reaches approximately 33.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 33.3 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C], a thermal zone that corresponds closely to the species' average active body temperature. This elevated oxygen consumption, typical of soricids, supports a lifestyle of near-constant foraging punctuated by brief periods of torpor when prey is scarce. The wet weight at birth for neonates is a mere 0.83 grams [Wwb = 0.83 grams], reflecting an extreme degree of altricial development common among shrews. Newborns emerge from the birth canal as hairless, blind pups weighing less than one gram, requiring sustained maternal investment during the first weeks of life. This neonatal mass is notably low even among small-bodied soricids, underscoring the trade-off between producing large litters and provisioning each offspring adequately.

Following parturition, the neonatal mammal enters a brief period of intense dependency. The mother initiates lactation almost immediately after delivery, and the suckling juveniles rely entirely on milk for nutritional support during the pre-weaning phase. Under the same thermoneutral conditions of 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C], the time since birth at weaning is approximately 22 days [tx = approximately 22 days], meaning that by the end of the third week the pups begin transitioning to solid food. This relatively early weaning age reflects the high maternal metabolic load imposed by concurrent lactation and thermoregulatory costs. Field records indicate that the gestation time for this species is 25 days [tg = 25 days] at 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C], a short gestation period consistent with the rapid reproductive turnover characteristic of shrews. The timing of these early life stages—from conception through weaning—is tightly compressed, allowing females to complete multiple breeding cycles within a single season when environmental conditions are favorable.

Sexual maturation in this species proceeds rapidly after weaning, a pattern linked to the high extrinsic mortality faced by small insectivores. At a thermoneutral 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C], puberty is attained at 46 days since birth [tp = 46 days since birth], meaning that young shrews become reproductively viable only a few weeks after achieving nutritional independence. This remarkably early age at sexual maturity enables individuals born early in the spring to breed during the same season, a life-history strategy common among mammals with short generation times. Once mature, individuals approach an ultimate wet weight of 14 grams [Wwi = 14 grams], representing the maximum adult body mass attained by this species. There is minimal sexual dimorphism in size, with both sexes converging on this asymptotic mass by early adulthood. The energetic costs of sustaining such a small but metabolically active body necessitate continual foraging, and territory sizes are consequently large relative to body mass.

Reproductive output in Blarina carolinensis is a direct function of both litter size and litter frequency. Females produce litters of 2 to 6 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2 to 6 pups per litter], with the modal litter size recorded at 4 offspring across much of the species range. Each year, females complete 2 to 3 litters annually [F_R_i = 2 to 3 litters annually], resulting in a total annual fecundity of between 6 and 18 pups per breeding season depending on food availability and local climate. This high reproductive rate is characteristic of soricids and counterbalances the elevated mortality associated with their small body size and high metabolic turnover. The timing of reproductive events is strongly tied to the thermal environment: ovulation and successful copulation occur most reliably when ambient temperatures approach 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C], as cooler conditions suppress activity in this predominantly fossorial species.

Longevity data for wild populations are limited, but records from captive colonies and mark-recapture studies provide a reliable estimate of maximum lifespan. At a thermoneutral 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C], the oldest documented individual survived for 803 days [am = 803 days], although most free-living animals likely succumb to predation or starvation well before reaching this age. This short lifespan—just over two years—is consistent with the rapid life-history pace predicted by the species' high metabolic output. The basal oxygen consumption of 33.3 milliliters per hour [JOi = 33.3 milliliters per hour] underlies this accelerated schedule: the high energetic cost of living in such a small package constrains both somatic maintenance and repair, contributing to early senescence at a temperature of 34.2 °C [T = 34.2 °C]. Comparative data from other soricids suggest that the maximum reproductive rate observed in the Southern short-tailed shrew represents an evolutionary optimum balancing litter size, weaning success, and maternal survival in a resource-variable environment.
